q: What is perplexity?
short: The exponential of the average negative log-likelihood per token on held-out text: the effective number of equally likely choices; lower means better next-token prediction.
follow: Why not use it for chatbots?

q: BLEU vs ROUGE?
short: BLEU is precision-oriented (clipped n-gram precision with a brevity penalty), used for translation; ROUGE is recall-oriented (n-gram recall, LCS), used for summarisation.

q: What does BERTScore measure?
short: Semantic similarity between candidate and reference by matching each token to its most similar token in the other text using contextual embeddings and averaging cosine similarities into precision, recall and F1.

q: How do human-preference arenas rank models?
short: Users compare anonymous pairs of answers and vote; ratings are fit with Elo or Bradley–Terry so that rating differences predict win probabilities.
mistakes: Treating arena rank as task accuracy.

q: What is LLM-as-a-judge?
short: Using a strong LLM to grade outputs against a rubric or compare two outputs, enabling scalable evaluation of open-ended tasks.

q: How do you measure hallucination?
short: Decompose outputs into atomic claims and verify each against a knowledge source or the provided context (factual precision, faithfulness), plus targeted benchmarks of known-answer questions.

q: What is benchmark contamination?
short: Test items (or close paraphrases) present in training data, letting models memorise answers and inflating scores.

q: Candidate 10 words, reference 8, 6 matches: P, R, F1?
Why can a fluent wrong answer score well on ROUGE?
short: ROUGE counts overlapping words/sequences regardless of meaning or truth; an answer reusing the reference's vocabulary with a wrong number or negation can share most n-grams.

q: List LLM-judge biases and mitigations.
short: Position (swap orders), verbosity (length-controlled comparisons, rubric emphasis), self-preference (different judge family), leniency/inconsistency (clear rubrics, examples, multiple judges), weak expertise (references, tools); calibrate on human labels.

q: Evaluate a RAG chatbot end to end.
short: Retrieval: recall@k and context precision on labelled queries. Generation: faithfulness, answer relevance, correctness, citation accuracy (LLM judge + human sample). System: latency, cost, refusal rate. Online: user feedback and escalations.

q: Elo: A at 1600, B at 1400. Expected score for A?
Static vs live benchmarks?
short: Static: fixed, cheap, reproducible, comparable over time, but saturate and leak. Live: refreshed questions resist contamination and track current ability, but are less comparable over time and costlier.

q: How should human evaluation be designed?
short: Clear guidelines with examples, trained raters, multiple ratings per item, blind and randomised order, pairwise comparisons, agreement measurement (κ), and adjudication of disagreements.

q: When is perplexity still useful?
short: Comparing pre-training runs or architectures on the same data and tokenizer, monitoring training, detecting domain shift or contamination (unusually low perplexity on test items), and scoring candidate texts.

q: Build an evaluation pipeline for weekly model updates.
short: Versioned test suites (capabilities, task-specific, safety, regression cases), automatic metrics and calibrated LLM judges, statistical significance and variance across seeds, human review of diffs, contamination checks, dashboards, and release gates.
mistakes: Changing the test set every week.

q: How can contamination be detected without access to training data?
short: Compare performance on original vs paraphrased/perturbed or post-cut-off items, test whether the model can complete benchmark items verbatim, examine perplexity anomalies, and use canary strings.

q: Why might an aligned chat model have higher perplexity than its base model?
short: Alignment shifts the distribution toward helpful assistant-style responses and away from imitating raw web text, so it predicts generic text less sharply even though it's more useful.
detail: Perplexity measures fit to the evaluation text.
mistakes: Concluding alignment made the model worse.

q: How do you evaluate an evaluator (meta-evaluation)?
short: Measure agreement between the metric/judge and careful human judgements (correlation, accuracy on pairwise preferences), test robustness to adversarial outputs (length padding, flattery), and check consistency across orders and runs.
mistakes: Assuming a strong model is a good judge.

q: Measure hallucination in long-form answers at scale.
short: Automatically extract atomic claims, retrieve evidence per claim, verify with an NLI model or LLM judge, compute supported fraction and count of unsupported claims, sample for human audit, and track by topic.
